periods.activity_title: Weave a Mat, Discover the Rule

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us make paper mats, p.92
tasks_in_class.description: Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips in alternating 1-under-1-over / 1-over-1-under pattern to make a mat.
Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven by studying the first two rows and writing the pattern rule.
Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper; complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.

time_bands.activity: Distribute coloured paper strips and a folded base sheet. Students work through Let us make paper mats, p.92 ("Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips...."), physically weaving the alternating over-under sequence to produce a small mat.

Hold up the 2-over-1-under mat from Q2, p.93 ("Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven...."). In pairs, students study the first two rows and write the row-by-row rule, then share and compare descriptions.
Students transfer to grid paper for Let Us Try, p.93 ("Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper...."), completing the full grid design by applying the rule they have just articulated.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is weaving every strip the same way (all over-under starting from the same side), producing a parallel-stripe rather than a checkerboard — pause after the first two strips and have students compare their mat to a neighbour's. Additional practice with progressively complex rules: Q3, p.93 (weave using the 4-row rule given) and Q4, p.93 (work out the steps for either shown weave design) can be assigned as follow-up work.
materials: Coloured paper strips (two colours per student)

tasks_in_class.description: Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap; count how many fit together.
Try fitting square cutouts around a point without any gap or overlap; count how many squares are needed.
Can 5 squares fit together around a point without gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point; count how many fit together without gaps or overlaps.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the term 'regular shape' (equal sides, equal angles). Ask students to sort the cutout set by shape before the activity begins.
Students work with triangle cutouts — Find Out, p.94 ("Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point....") — arranging them around a central point on plain paper and counting how many fit with no gap.

Repeat with square cutouts — Find Out, p.94 ("Try fitting square cutouts around a point....") — counting squares needed, then test whether a fifth square could fit — Find Out, p.94 ("Can 5 squares fit together around a point...."). Groups articulate why or why not and share.

Students try hexagon cutouts — Find Out, p.94 ("Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point....") — recording how many fit. Class compares all three shapes and discusses which ones tile the plane without gaps.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent confusion is thinking that any regular shape tessellates; the pentagon and octagon counter-examples are the payoff of the reasoning here — connecting back to the count of shapes around a point helps students see why the gap appears. Ensure cutouts are accurately sized (pre-cut or traced from templates) so that measurement error does not mislead the exploration.
materials: Pre-cut regular triangle cutouts (at least 8 per group)
Pre-cut square cutouts (at least 6 per group)
Pre-cut regular hexagon cutouts (at least 4 per group)

periods.activity_title: Shapes That Gap and Patterns That Continue

tasks_in_class.description: Try drawing regular octagons together to check whether they tessellate without gaps or overlaps.
Identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern; continue the pattern on the grid and colour it appropriately.
Identify shapes meeting at marked points in the octagon+square tiling; check if same shapes meet at all points; continue and colour the pattern.
In the square+triangle tiling: identify shapes at marked points; check consistency; continue and colour it; reason whether triangles are equilateral.

homework.description: Create similar tiling patterns using other cutouts of shapes.

time_bands.activity: Students try drawing octagons side-by-side — Find Out, p.95 ("Try drawing regular octagons together....") — and observe the gaps that appear. They name the shape left over and discuss why octagons alone do not fill the plane.

Using the book's grid, students identify the two shapes in the mixed pattern — Find Out, p.95 ("Identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern....") — then continue it for at least two more rows and colour it.

Students move to the octagon+square tiling — Find Out, p.96 ("Identify shapes meeting at marked points in the octagon+square tiling....") — checking whether the same shapes meet at every marked point, then continuing and colouring.

Students work through the square+triangle tiling — Find Out, p.96 ("In the square+triangle tiling: identify shapes....") — reasoning whether the triangles are equilateral by comparing side lengths visible on the grid.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often skip the 'check consistency at all points' step and just colour; prompt them to compare two different interior points before they colour, so they build the habit of verification. The home task Find Out, p.96 asks students to create their own tiling with other shape cutouts and can be brought in for display without any class-time dependency.

tasks_in_class.description: Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify the geometrical shapes created.
How many different types of triangles can you make with 2 rhombus pieces? Observe and measure their sides; what do you notice?
Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle) from the rhombus pieces?
Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal (scalene) from the rhombus pieces?
Cut equilateral triangle; fold to check all angles are equal; cut in half; observe the resulting scalene triangle and check its angles.

time_bands.activity: Students cut their rhombus sheet into four congruent triangles — Try This, p.97 ("Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together....") — then try all arrangements of two pieces and trace the shapes formed.

Working from Try This Q1, p.97 ("How many different types of triangles can you make...."), students measure the sides of each triangle formed and record equal or unequal sides, arriving at the terms isosceles and equilateral through their own observations.

Students test Try This Q2, p.97 ("Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal....") and Try This Q3, p.97 ("Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal....") with their pieces, and reason aloud or in writing about what the rhombus's side lengths allow.

Students fold and cut the equilateral triangle as in Try This, p.97 ("Cut equilateral triangle; fold to check all angles are equal...."), comparing the resulting scalene halves to the isosceles triangles from the rhombus.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'different-looking' with 'different type' — two triangles that look like mirror images are the same type; encourage measurement to settle the question rather than visual judgment alone. A common error is assuming two pieces always make a triangle; tracing all arrangements and counting sides of each shape prevents this.
materials: Pre-drawn rhombus sheet (one per student, with diagonals marked for cutting)

periods.activity_title: Three and Four Pieces — Building Polygons

tasks_in_class.description: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make by fitting 2 rhombus triangles? Explore the possibilities.
Measure sides of quadrilaterals A and B; find equal pairs (adjacent or opposite); identify what types of angles each has.
Use 3 rhombus triangles to form shapes; count sides of each; try creating a 3-sided, 4-sided, and 5-sided shape.
Use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, pentagon, hexagon, octagon) can be made.

homework.description: Draw two different kites and two different parallelograms in the grid given.

time_bands.activity: Students use two rhombus triangles to find all distinct quadrilaterals — Try This Q4, p.98 ("How many different 4-sided shapes can you make....") — tracing each arrangement before moving to the next.

For Try This Q5, p.98 ("Measure sides of quadrilaterals A and B...."), students measure and label equal sides and note whether equal sides are adjacent or opposite, then name the type of angle at each vertex.

With three pieces, students attempt Try This Q7, p.99 ("Use 3 rhombus triangles to form shapes...."), recording the number of sides for each shape they build and checking whether a 3-sided and a 5-sided shape are achievable.
All four pieces go together for Try This Q8, p.99 ("Use all 4 rhombus pieces; find which shapes...."). Students tick off which named polygons they can form, comparing results with a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often mistake a kite for a rhombus because both have four equal sides in some arrangements; prompt them to check whether equal sides are adjacent or opposite to distinguish the two. Try This Q6, p.99 (drawing kites and parallelograms on a grid) is assigned as home practice to consolidate this distinction.
materials: Rhombus triangle pieces from the previous cutting activity (or fresh pre-cut sets)

periods.activity_title: Tangrams, Property Cards, and Paper Kites

tasks_in_class.description: Cut out tangram shapes; compare sides and angles of each piece; use some or all pieces to make the given shapes (parallelogram, rectangle, triangle, trapezoid).
Match 7 property statements to the correct shape from: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram. Note shapes that match more than one statement.
Make a kite by paper-folding from a square (fold diagonal, fold corner A then B inward); observe what shapes appear inside the kite.

time_bands.activity: Students cut the tangram — Tangram, p.99 ("Cut out tangram shapes; compare sides and angles....") — examine each piece, then assemble the given target shapes (parallelogram, rectangle, triangle, trapezoid), tracing each completed arrangement.

Individually, students work through Which Shape Am I?, p.100 ("Match 7 property statements to the correct shape...."), writing the shape name beside each statement and flagging any statement that applies to more than one shape. A brief share-out consolidates the kite/parallelogram/rhombus distinctions.

Each student folds a square sheet into a kite — Kites, p.100 ("Make a kite by paper-folding from a square....") — then opens it to identify the triangles and symmetry line inside, discussing what properties the kite has that they can now name.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in 'Which Shape Am I?' is marking only one shape per statement and missing that a square satisfies all rectangle properties — encourage students to check every shape against each statement. When folding the kite, the order of folds (diagonal first, then corners) is critical; a quick demonstration before students begin prevents a ragged result.
materials: Square paper (one sheet per student for kite-folding)

section_titles: Play with Circles and Circle Designs
periods.activity_title: Diameters Make Rectangles; Points Make Designs

tasks_in_class.description: Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints; check the shape and angles formed; try with different diameter pairs.
Join numbered circle points (1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, ...) to make a string-art design; think of a way to make the overlapping-circles image.

time_bands.activity: Students draw a circle with a compass, mark two diameters, and join the four endpoints — Play with Circles, p.101 ("Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters....") — then measure or fold to check the angles. They repeat with a different pair of diameters and compare shapes, leading to the conjecture that joining diameter endpoints always gives a rectangle.

Using the numbered-circle worksheet, students join points following the skip-rule — Circle Designs, p.101 ("Join numbered circle points (1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, ....)") — building their string-art design step by step. They observe the shape emerging and attempt to sketch how the overlapping-circles design might be constructed.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often draw diameters that are perpendicular and get a square, then assume any diameter pair gives a square; prompt them to try diameters at a different angle so they see the general rectangle, not just the special case. For the circle design, count the points aloud as a class once through the rule before students draw, so the skip pattern is clear.
materials: Numbered-circle worksheet (pre-printed or drawn: circle with 12 equally spaced numbered points)

periods.activity_title: Nets, Missing Cubes, and a Painted Puzzle

tasks_in_class.description: Given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position in the net.
Given three big solid cube frames with holes, work out how many small cubes have been removed from each (a, b, c).
Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red; find how many small cubes have 3/2/1/0 painted faces.

time_bands.activity: Students study the three views in Cube Connections Q1, p.102 ("Given three views of a cube with different face patterns...."), mentally rotating the cube to decide which view corresponds to which face of the net, then draw the pattern on each face.

For Cube Connections Q2, p.102 ("Given three big solid cube frames with holes...."), students count the small cubes present in each frame and subtract from the full-cube total to find how many were removed from each of the three frames.

Students tackle the painted-cube problem — Cube Connections Q3, p.102 ("Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube....") — by sketching or describing the positions: corners, edges, face-centres, and interior, then counting each type systematically.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in the painted-cube problem is double-counting edge cubes as corner cubes; encourage students to draw and label the three layers of the 3×3×3 cube (top, middle, bottom) before counting each category. The shape-arrangement puzzle from p.102 (Tanu's 7 shapes) is equally rich and is held back to give the spatial reasoning tasks space.
materials: Cube net printout (one per student, for Q1)
Small unit-cube models or linking cubes (optional, for Q2 and Q3 visualisation)

tasks_in_class.description: Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes (2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle) in a line.

time_bands.activity: Read the puzzle aloud together — Puzzle, p.102 ("Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes...."). Students make a working strip of 7 boxes (drawn or cut) to hold shape labels, and read all five clues once before placing anything.

Working in pairs, students apply clues one at a time, placing shapes and using elimination to narrow possibilities. Encourage them to note when a clue rules out a position rather than fixing one, building systematic deductive reasoning.

Pairs share their completed arrangement and the order in which they applied the clues. Class discusses whether a different clue sequence would have been more efficient, and checks the unique solution against all five clues.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently try to apply all five clues simultaneously, which leads to confusion; suggest they start with the most restrictive clue (the one that limits to fewest positions) and build from there. If a pair finishes early, prompt them to write their own shape-in-a-line puzzle with three clues for a partner to solve.
materials: Printed or hand-drawn 7-box strip per student pair
Small shape cut-outs or labelled pieces (2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle)

tasks_in_class.description: Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models; observe face shapes, faces at each vertex, and count edges for each solid.

time_bands.activity: Briefly discuss the cube and cuboid as known 3D solids — what shape are their faces, how many faces meet at a corner? This activates the language of faces, vertices, and edges before students encounter the new solids.

Students cut and fold the nets from the back of the book — Icosahedron and Dodecahedron, p.103 ("Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models....") — working carefully to score fold lines and glue tabs in sequence to form closed models.

Holding their completed models, students answer the observation questions from p.103: name the face shape, check whether all faces are the same, count how many faces meet at one vertex, and count total edges for each solid. Pairs compare their counts and resolve any discrepancies.

periods.teacher_notes: Counting edges on the completed model is surprisingly difficult; suggest students mark each counted edge with a pencil dot so none is counted twice. Students often struggle with the net fold order — advise them to fold and score all lines before applying glue, and to start closing the solid from the base row upward.
materials: Net sheets from the back of the textbook (icosahedron and dodecahedron, one set per student)

section_titles: Play with Circles and Circle Designs
periods.activity_title: Shapes, Patterns, and Properties — Chapter Synthesis

time_bands.activity: Pattern gallery: On the board (or cards), display four incomplete patterns — a weave row, a tessellation row, a circle skip-sequence, and a 2-over-1-under row. Students, working individually, write the next step of each and name the rule. Discuss as a class.

Shape-property sort: Each student receives a card showing one shape (equilateral triangle, isosceles triangle, scalene triangle, kite, rhombus, rectangle, square, regular hexagon, cube, icosahedron). They write two properties that name and distinguish their shape, then the class assembles the cards into a wall-chart grouping 2D/3D, polygon/non-polygon, and tessellates/does not tessellate.

Synthesis challenge: Pose two connecting questions: (1) A 3×3×3 cube is built from small cubes — which position (corner, edge, face, or inside) appears in both the painted-cube problem and in the arrangement of faces on a cube net? Students reason aloud. (2) Which shapes from the weaving and tessellation sections also appear as faces of the icosahedron and dodecahedron? Students match shape names across sections.

Exit question (individual, written): Name one shape you can make from rhombus triangles that also appears in a tessellating pattern, and explain in one sentence why it tessellates. Teacher collects slips as an informal check of integrated understanding.

periods.teacher_notes: The synthesis unit draws on the full conceptual vocabulary of the chapter — weave rules, regular shapes, triangle classification, quadrilateral properties, circle constructions, cube net reasoning, and polyhedra properties — so the connecting questions in the third band should be kept open, not leading. The exit slip is a lightweight written check; accept any well-reasoned shape-tessellation pairing (e.g., equilateral triangle from rhombus pieces tessellates because six fit around a point without a gap).
materials: Shape-property cards (one per student, printed or hand-written)
Board or display space for the wall-chart
Plain paper slips for exit question

items.prompt: On the grid on p.92, shade the squares to show a 1-over-1-under weave pattern for the first three rows. Use two colours — one for the strip and one for the background.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: shaded-unshaded-shaded-unshaded... Row 2: unshaded-shaded-unshaded-shaded... Row 3: same as Row 1. The colours alternate in a checkerboard arrangement.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the alternating over-under rule: each row reverses the starting position of the previous row.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a completed Row 1 to copy and continue; stretch: ask them to show what Row 4 and Row 5 would look like and name the repeating unit.

exercise.book_ref: Let us make paper mats, p.92
exercise.description: Fold coloured paper, cut slits, and weave 8 strips in alternating 1-under-1-over / 1-over-1-under pattern to make a mat.

items.prompt: Riya places equilateral triangle cutouts around a single point with no gaps and no overlaps. How many triangles meet at that point?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 equilateral triangles meet at a point with no gaps or overlaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each interior angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°; six such angles fill the full 360° around a point.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of squares meeting at a point (4 squares) and applying that count to triangles.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be guessing without systematic counting, or confusing the number of sides with the number of shapes.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be doubling the correct count, possibly thinking of two layers or confusing edge-count with vertex-count.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let them physically arrange paper triangle cutouts around a point and count; stretch: ask how many angles each triangle contributes and what the total must be for a complete fit.

exercise.description: Fit regular triangle cutouts around a point without any gap; count how many fit together.

items.prompt: Rohan places regular hexagon cutouts around a single point with no gaps and no overlaps. How many hexagons fit at that point?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 regular hexagons meet at a point with no gaps or overlaps.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Each interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120°; three such angles sum to 360°, filling the space around a point exactly.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think two hexagons share a side at a point and confuse side-sharing with vertex-meeting.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be applying the count for squares (4) to hexagons without testing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be recalling that 6 triangles meet at a point and transferring that number without reasoning about the different angle size.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use hexagon cutouts on paper and count; stretch: ask what angle each hexagon contributes and verify the total equals 360°.

exercise.description: Try fitting regular hexagon cutouts at a point; count how many fit together without gaps or overlaps.

items.prompt: Priya tries to tile a floor using only regular octagon tiles. She notices a gap appears between the tiles. What shape is the gap? Draw or describe it.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The gap is a square. When regular octagons are placed together, the spaces left between them are squares.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Observe the shape of the leftover space after placing octagons side-by-side: four sides of equal length and right angles form a square.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student trace two octagons side-by-side and look at the enclosed space; stretch: ask why a square fills the gap exactly and what that tells us about how octagons and squares can be combined in a tiling.

exercise.description: Try drawing regular octagons together to check whether they tessellate without gaps or overlaps.

items.prompt: Arjun cuts a rhombus along both diagonals and gets four identical triangles. He joins two triangles along their longest side. Which shape does he most likely get?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A rhombus. Joining two identical triangles along their longest (shared diagonal) side reconstructs the original rhombus.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two congruent triangles placed along their equal longest sides form the original rhombus from which they were cut.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may confuse a rhombus with a square, not distinguishing that a rhombus has equal sides but angles that need not be right angles.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may think any four-sided shape with two pairs of equal sides is a rectangle, missing the requirement for right angles.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may not realise that joining two identical triangles along a full side creates a four-sided shape, not a triangle.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically cut and join the pieces; stretch: ask what other shape they can make by joining the two triangles along a different edge.

exercise.description: Cut rhombus triangular pieces; fit 2 together; trace and identify the geometrical shapes created.

items.prompt: Using two rhombus triangles, Meera makes a quadrilateral. She notices that two sides of the quadrilateral are longer than the other two. Name the type of quadrilateral she has made and describe where the equal sides are.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Meera has made a kite (or a parallelogram, depending on which edges are joined). In a kite, each pair of equal sides is adjacent to each other; in a parallelogram, equal sides are opposite each other.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the two pairs of equal sides are next to each other (adjacent — kite) or across from each other (opposite — parallelogram).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student label the four sides with letters and then mark pairs that are equal; stretch: ask them to make a second quadrilateral from the same two triangles and compare where the equal sides sit.

exercise.description: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make by fitting 2 rhombus triangles? Explore the possibilities.

items.prompt: Tara folds a square sheet of paper in half along a diagonal and then folds one corner inward. Which shape does she make?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A kite. Folding the diagonal and then folding a corner inward produces a four-sided shape with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The paper-folding from a square (fold diagonal, then fold corner inward) produces a kite with two pairs of equal adjacent sides.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may associate folding with rectangles because folding a rectangle in half gives a smaller rectangle, not recognising that diagonal folding changes the shape.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may confuse a kite with a rhombus; both have four sides but a rhombus has all four sides equal, while a kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides of different lengths.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be counting the fold lines as extra sides, arriving at five sides instead of four.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student fold an actual square and count the sides of the result; stretch: ask them to identify where the line of symmetry is in the kite they made.

exercise.description: Make a kite by paper-folding from a square (fold diagonal, fold corner A then B inward); observe what shapes appear inside the kite.

items.section_title: Play with Circles and Circle Designs
items.prompt: Vikram draws a circle and marks two diameters. He joins the four endpoints to form a shape. What shape is formed? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A rectangle (or a square in the special case when the diameters are perpendicular and equal in length, but always at least a rectangle). The four endpoints are equally distant from the centre, and the diagonals of the shape are two diameters — equal in length and bisecting each other — which is the property of a rectangle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The two diameters are equal in length and cross at the centre of the circle, so the shape formed has diagonals that are equal and bisect each other — the defining property of a rectangle.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw the shape, fold it along each diagonal, and check that the halves match; stretch: ask what happens when the two diameters are perpendicular and whether the shape is still a rectangle.

exercise.description: Draw a circle with compass; mark two diameters; join the four endpoints; check the shape and angles formed; try with different diameter pairs.

items.prompt: An icosahedron is built from a net of identical triangular faces. How many triangular faces does an icosahedron have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 20 triangular faces.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the triangular panels on the icosahedron net or model; the total is 20.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of an octahedron (8 faces) and confusing the two solids.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may be thinking of a dodecahedron (12 faces) and confusing which solid has triangular faces.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be counting edges (30) rather than faces.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student touch and count each face on the completed model; stretch: ask how many faces meet at each vertex of the icosahedron and whether this is the same at every vertex.

exercise.description: Use nets to build icosahedron and dodecahedron models; observe face shapes, faces at each vertex, and count edges for each solid.

items.prompt: A mat is woven using the rule: 2-over-1-under. Write out the weave sequence for Row 1 and Row 2. At which row does the pattern begin to repeat, and how do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: over-over-under-over-over-under… Row 2: under-over-over-under-over-over… Row 3: over-over-under… (same as Row 1). The pattern repeats at Row 3 because Row 3 is identical to Row 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the over/under sequence for each row until a row matches an earlier row exactly — that is the repeat point.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a partially completed table with Row 1 filled in; stretch: ask the student to predict how many rows before the pattern repeats if the rule were 3-over-1-under.

exercise.description: Figure out how the 2-over-1-under mat is woven by studying the first two rows and writing the pattern rule.

items.prompt: Sana tries to tile a surface using only regular pentagons. She finds it is impossible. Explain in one sentence why regular pentagons cannot tessellate on their own.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Regular pentagons cannot tessellate because the interior angle of a regular pentagon (108°) does not divide 360° evenly, so pentagons placed around a point always leave a gap or overlap.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the interior angle divides 360° without remainder; 360 ÷ 108 is not a whole number, so pentagons leave gaps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: tell the student the interior angle of a pentagon is 108° and ask whether 3 × 108°, 4 × 108°, etc. equal 360°; stretch: ask which other shape has an interior angle that divides 360° evenly and therefore tessellates.

exercise.description: Can 5 squares fit together around a point without gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?

items.prompt: Look at a tiling pattern that uses two different shapes. At every interior point, three hexagons and two triangles meet. Which statement best explains why no gap is left?

options.label: A
options.text: Both shapes have an even number of sides.

options.label: B
options.text: The angles of the shapes at each point add up to 360°.

options.label: C
options.text: The shapes are the same size, so they always fit together.

options.label: D
options.text: The sides of hexagons are longer than the sides of triangles.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The angles of the shapes at each point add up to 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: No gap exists at a meeting point when the angles of all shapes meeting there sum exactly to 360°.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses size with angular fit; shapes of the same size can still leave gaps if their angles do not sum to 360°.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student focuses on side length rather than angle, missing that tessellation depends on angle sum at a vertex, not side length comparison.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has found an incidental property (hexagons have 6 sides, triangles have 3) but this has no bearing on whether shapes fill space around a point.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student add the angles at one meeting point with a calculator or by repeated addition; stretch: ask them to find a second combination of shapes whose angles also sum to 360°.

exercise.description: Identify the two shapes in the given tessellating pattern; continue the pattern on the grid and colour it appropriately.

items.prompt: In a square-and-triangle tiling, the triangles fill the gaps between squares. Are these triangles equilateral? Write one reason for your answer.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, the triangles are equilateral because each of their sides is equal in length to the side of the square they share, and all three sides are the same length.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare each side of the triangle to the square's side on the grid; if all three match the square's side length, the triangle is equilateral.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use a ruler on the grid to measure all three sides of one triangle; stretch: ask them to explain why having three equal sides means all three angles are also equal.

exercise.description: In the square+triangle tiling: identify shapes at marked points; check consistency; continue and colour it; reason whether triangles are equilateral.

items.prompt: Kezia cuts a rhombus into four identical triangles using both diagonals. She fits two triangles together along one short side. What type of triangle does she get?

options.label: A
options.text: Equilateral triangle — all three sides are equal.

options.label: B
options.text: Isosceles triangle — exactly two sides are equal.

options.label: D
options.text: Scalene triangle — all three sides are different.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: An isosceles triangle — exactly two sides are equal.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Two identical right triangles joined along the short side produce an isosceles triangle with two equal legs and a longer base.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may not have measured the sides; in a rhombus with unequal diagonals the triangles are not equilateral.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student may be thinking of cutting an equilateral triangle in half, which gives a scalene triangle, but here the pieces come from a rhombus.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student identifies the right angle at the centre of the rhombus but names the whole resulting triangle by that property rather than by its side lengths.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student measure all three sides of the new triangle with a ruler; stretch: ask what type of triangle is formed if the two equal diagonals of a square are used instead.

exercise.description: How many different types of triangles can you make with 2 rhombus pieces? Observe and measure their sides; what do you notice?

items.prompt: Two rhombus triangles are placed together to form quadrilateral P. The sides of P are measured: two sides are 3 cm and two sides are 5 cm. Are the equal sides adjacent to each other or opposite each other? What is the name of quadrilateral P?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: If the two 3 cm sides are next to each other (adjacent) and the two 5 cm sides are next to each other, P is a kite. If the two 3 cm sides are across from each other (opposite) and the two 5 cm sides are opposite, P is a parallelogram.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify whether equal sides share a vertex (adjacent — kite) or face each other across the shape (opposite — parallelogram).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw and label the four sides then draw arrows connecting equal pairs; stretch: ask them to describe one angle property that further distinguishes a kite from a parallelogram.

exercise.description: Measure sides of quadrilaterals A and B; find equal pairs (adjacent or opposite); identify what types of angles each has.

items.prompt: Which of the following statements is true for a rectangle but NOT for every parallelogram?

options.label: A
options.text: All four angles are right angles.

options.label: C
options.text: Opposite sides are equal in length.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: All four angles are right angles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A rectangle is a special parallelogram with right angles; a general parallelogram can have any angles as long as opposite ones are equal.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has identified a property shared by ALL parallelograms, not just rectangles — opposite sides being equal is not unique to rectangles.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has again identified a property of ALL parallelograms; opposite sides being parallel defines a parallelogram, not specifically a rectangle.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Diagonals bisecting each other is true of all parallelograms, including rectangles, so this property does not distinguish a rectangle from the general case.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a parallelogram and a rectangle side by side and ask the student to compare angles with a corner of a book; stretch: ask whether a square satisfies all the properties of a rectangle and explain why.

exercise.description: Match 7 property statements to the correct shape from: square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram. Note shapes that match more than one statement.

items.prompt: A cube net is unfolded flat. The top face of the cube shows a circle. On the flat net, which face will be directly opposite the circle face when the net is folded? Describe how you worked it out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The face directly opposite the circle is the one that, in the net, is separated from the circle face by exactly two faces in a straight strip (the face two steps away along the central column of a cross-shaped net). The exact position depends on the net layout shown in the book, but the method is to trace the folding path and identify which face ends up across the interior of the cube from the circle.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Mentally fold the net step by step, tracking which face lands opposite the marked face after all folds are complete.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student cut out the net and physically fold it; stretch: ask them to mark a second face and identify its opposite as well.

exercise.description: Given three views of a cube with different face patterns, draw each face on the correct position in the net.

items.prompt:
Tanu places 7 shapes in a row: 2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, and 1 rectangle. Use these two clues to work out where the circle is placed:
• The circle is between the two squares.
• The hexagon is at one end of the row.
In which position (1st, 2nd, 3rd, …, 7th) is the circle?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The circle is in position 4 (the middle). With the hexagon at one end (position 1 or 7) and the circle between the two squares, the only arrangement that places the circle centrally between both squares is position 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix the hexagon at an end, then place both squares symmetrically around position 4, which forces the circle to position 4.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student 7 labelled slips and ask them to try placing physically; stretch: ask them to write a third clue that would uniquely determine the position of the rectangle.

exercise.description: Use 5 clues to find Tanu's arrangement of 7 shapes (2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, 1 rectangle) in a line.

items.prompt: A student starts drawing a weave pattern on a grid using the rule 1-over-1-under. Row 1 starts: shaded, unshaded, shaded, unshaded, shaded. What is the correct sequence for Row 2?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Unshaded, shaded, unshaded, shaded, unshaded — Row 2 reverses the starting position of Row 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: In a 1-over-1-under weave, each row shifts by one so the first square of Row 2 is the opposite colour to the first square of Row 1.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has repeated Row 1 exactly, not seeing that the alternating rule shifts by one position each row.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has grouped the shaded and unshaded squares in pairs rather than alternating them singly.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has grouped unshaded and shaded in pairs, a similar pairing error in a different arrangement.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: give the student a completed Row 1 on grid paper and ask them to colour Row 2 by placing strips; stretch: ask what Row 3 looks like and whether they can predict Row 10.

exercise.description: Draw the given weave pattern on grid paper; complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.

items.prompt: On the dot grid on p.99, draw two different kites. Label the two pairs of equal adjacent sides on each kite.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Two kites are drawn on the grid with vertices on dot intersections. Each kite has one pair of shorter equal adjacent sides and one pair of longer equal adjacent sides, with the equal-side pairs meeting at a vertex. The labels identify each pair.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place the kite's axis of symmetry along a grid line, then place pairs of equal adjacent sides symmetrically on each side of the axis.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: provide a completed example kite for reference and ask the student to draw just one different kite; stretch: ask the student to also draw two parallelograms and compare where the equal sides sit in each shape.

exercise.description: Draw two different kites and two different parallelograms in the grid given.

items.prompt: A solid 3×3×3 cube is made up of small unit cubes. A tunnel of 1×1 squares is drilled straight through the middle of the cube from front to back, removing a column of 3 small cubes. How many small cubes remain in the solid?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 24 small cubes remain. The full cube has 27 small cubes. Drilling a 1×1 tunnel straight through from front to back removes 3 small cubes (one per layer), leaving 27 − 3 = 24.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the number of cubes removed (one per layer × 3 layers = 3) from the total number in the full cube (3 × 3 × 3 = 27).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student draw or build the three layers and shade the removed cubes; stretch: ask how many cubes remain if tunnels are drilled through the middle from front-to-back AND from left-to-right (one cube is shared by both tunnels).

exercise.description: Given three big solid cube frames with holes, work out how many small cubes have been removed from each (a, b, c).

items.prompt: A 3×3×3 cube is built from 27 small unit cubes and all six outer faces are painted red. How many small cubes have exactly 2 faces painted red?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12 small cubes have exactly 2 faces painted. These are the edge-cubes (not at corners): each edge of the large cube has 3 small cubes, but the 2 corner cubes on each edge are corner-cubes (3 painted faces). Only the middle cube on each edge has exactly 2 painted faces. A cube has 12 edges, so there are 12 × 1 = 12 such cubes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the small cubes that sit on an edge but not at a corner: each of the 12 edges of the large cube contributes exactly 1 such cube, giving 12.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student sketch the top layer as a 3×3 grid and shade the edge-but-not-corner squares, then count; stretch: ask them to verify that 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27 and explain what each number represents.

exercise.description: Nisha glues 27 small cubes into a 3×3×3 cube and paints it red; find how many small cubes have 3/2/1/0 painted faces.
